items.currentCitation: KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Compromise speech (1895); Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute; Washington's financial patronage from Carnegie and Rockefeller; Du Bois's concept of the "Talented Tenth"; founding of the NAACP (1909) by Du Bois, Ida B. Wells, Mary Church Terrell, and others; Library of Congress, NAACP Records (loc.gov) magazine (founded 1910); Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) and the legal structure of Jim Crow; documented lynching statistics from the era (Wells's Southern Horrors, 1892); Washington's "Atlanta Compromise" and its political trade-offs for Black political rights. A top-scoring response states a defensible claim — either position is acceptable if well-argued. A student arguing for Du Bois uses the excerpt's enumeration of three specific failures (disfranchisement, legal inferiority, withdrawal of educational funding) that occurred during Washington's "triumphant" period as evidence that accommodation produced no tangible gains. Outside knowledge evidence: the founding of the NAACP (1909) as a direct response to Washington's approach, Du Bois's Crisis magazine, and the legal challenges to Jim Crow laws. A student arguing for Washington might use Tuskegee's tangible record of graduates entering skilled trades, Washington's ability to secure Gilded Age patronage from industrialists like Carnegie, and the danger of direct protest in an era of widespread lynching. Strong reasoning synthesizes: both strategies were constrained by the same hostile environment, and the debate itself reveals the impossible position of Black Americans trying to achieve equality within a system that had formally committed itself to white supremacy.

items.currentCitation: KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896); the Atlanta Compromise (1895) and Tuskegee's practical industrial training record; Du Bois's "Talented Tenth" concept; founding of the NAACP (1909); Library of Congress, NAACP Records (loc.gov) magazine (1910); Wells's documentation of lynching statistics and her exile from Memphis; the Great Migration (ca. 1910-1930) as a structural response to Southern racial terror; Wilson's segregation of the federal civil service (1913); lynching continued despite NAACP campaigns for federal anti-lynching legislation (repeatedly blocked in Congress 1918-1922); the 15th Amendment's failure to protect Black voting rights in practice. A top-scoring response argues that while Washington, Du Bois, and Wells each represented a distinct and internally coherent strategy, none produced lasting structural change by 1920 — because all three were operating against a system of racial exclusion that was legally entrenched (Plessy v. Ferguson, 1896), economically reinforced (disenfranchisement, sharecropping), and protected by organized violence (lynching). HIPP Document 1 — Washington: Historical context: speaking at a moment of maximum vulnerability for Black Southerners — Reconstruction has ended, Plessy is one year away, and lynching is at its peak; Intended audience: both white Southerners whose approval Washington needed and Black Southerners he was counseling; Purpose: to secure the political survival of Black institutions within a white-supremacist system; POV: a man born into slavery who saw industrial education as a realistic survival strategy given the absence of federal protection — revealing the context-dependence of his "accommodationism." Document 2 — Du Bois: Historical context: seven years after the Atlanta Compromise, with disfranchisement, legal inferiority, and educational withdrawal documented; Audience: Black intellectuals and sympathetic whites; Purpose: to demolish the theoretical foundation of accommodation by showing its measurable failures; POV: a Harvard-trained academic who could analyze macro trends Washington's institution-building could not address — but whose protest strategy also had limited structural leverage without federal enforcement. Document 3 — Wells: Historical context: 1892 — peak of lynching era, the same year she was driven from Memphis; Audience: "the white man's sense of justice" — framing the appeal for political survival; Purpose: to document racial terror using factual evidence to make it impossible to deny; POV: a journalist using the tools of her trade to challenge a system — but one who also recognized the limits of moral appeal when violence was state-sanctioned. Outside knowledge: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) as constitutional sanction for racial exclusion; the founding of the NAACP (1909) as institutionalization of Du Bois's protest strategy; continued lynching statistics (3,000+ documented lynchings 1882-1930); the Great Migration beginning ca. 1910 as Black Americans' ultimate strategic response to Southern racial terror — voting with their feet.
